verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand, and made his defense.
“I think myself happy, King Agrippa, that I am to make my defense before you today concerning all the things that I am accused by the Jews,
especially because you are expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently.
“Indeed, all the Jews know my way of life from my youth up, which was from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem;
having known me from the first, if they are willing to testify, that after the strictest sect of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
Now I stand here to be judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. Concerning this hope I am accused by the Jews, King Agrippa!
Why is it judged incredible with you, if God does raise the dead?
“I myself most certainly thought that I ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
This I also did in Jerusalem. I both shut up many of the saints in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were put to death I gave my vote against them.
Punishing them often in all the synagogues, I tried to make them blaspheme. Being exceedingly enraged against them, I persecuted them even to foreign cities.
“Whereupon as I traveled to Damascus with the authority and commission from the chief priests,
at noon, O king, I saw on the way a light from the sky, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those who traveled with me.
When we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’
“I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ “He said, ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

But arise, and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things which you have seen, and of the things which I will reveal to you;
delivering you from the people, and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you,

to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive remission of sins and an inheritance among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’
“Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision,
but declared first to them of Damascus, at Jerusalem, and throughout all the country of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, doing works worthy of repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple, and tried to kill me.
Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would happen,
how the Christ must suffer, and how, by the resurrection of the dead, he would be first to proclaim light both to these people and to the Gentiles.”
As he thus made his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are crazy! Your great learning is driving you insane!”
But he said, “I am not crazy, most excellent Festus, but boldly declare words of truth and reasonableness.
For the king knows of these things, to whom also I speak freely. For I am persuaded that none of these things is hidden from him, for this has not been done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?”
Paul said, “I pray to God, that whether with little or with much, not only you, but also all that hear me today, might become such as I am, except for these bonds.”
The king rose up with the governor, and Bernice, and those who sat with them.
When they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing worthy of death or of bonds.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “This man might have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

footnotes.content: Agrippa gives Paul the floor—notice the courtesy even in captivity. There is a strange honor in being heard by a king, and Paul will not squander it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Happy to answer," Paul says. What a posture: not bitter under false accusation, but grateful for the chance to speak. The Lord's joy can live in us even when we're on trial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul knows Agrippa is expert in Jewish law and custom, so he speaks to him from that ground. He asks for patience—a gift he gives in return. Real persuasion begins with respect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul roots his defense in his own history: a life lived openly, known from childhood in Jerusalem. There is power in an examined life, one that can stand the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He was a Pharisee—the strictest sect. He lived it without hiding. When God turns us around, we don't deny our past; we carry it as a witness to how far His mercy reaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul is not on trial for his faith, he claims—he's on trial for *hope*. The promise made to the fathers is the same one he now stakes his life on. That continuity, that faithfulness, is his anchor.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hoping to attain the promise. He speaks of Israel's longing as though it belongs to him still—which it does. He has not left his people; he has fulfilled their deepest prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why would it seem incredible that God raises the dead?" A simple question that cuts to the root: if God is who He claims, nothing is beyond His power. Paul turns the court's disbelief into its own absurdity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He was certain he *ought* to oppose Jesus. Conviction without Christ is blind certainty; that is what he confesses now. There is gentleness in how he admits his old zeal was sincere but wrongly aimed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shut up saints in prison, gave his vote for their death. He speaks these terrible deeds plainly, without excusing them. Repentance can name what it did; shame tries to hide it. He hides nothing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He punished them in synagogues, tried to force them to blaspheme, pursued them to foreign cities. His old fervor was misdirected rage. Yet the Lord caught him at the height of his own certainty and turned him around—that is always how it happens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He carried official papers to Damascus—legal cover for a hunt. Even his credentials were a trap, yet the Lord would meet him there anyway. No place is too dark for Him to break through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A light at noon brighter than the sun—the risen Jesus blazes past all reason, all argument. It is not a debate. It is the Lord Himself, and one look unmakes everything Paul thought he knew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Saul, Saul"—the doubled name, as when God called Abraham, Moses. He hears his own name from the glory. The voice speaks Hebrew, his mother tongue, making it intimate and inescapable. Then: "It is hard for you to kick against the goads."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Who are you, Lord?" All his learning, all his certainty, melts to this one honest question. And Jesus answers: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting." The persecutor finds he has been striking at the King himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rise and stand on your feet—not as a victim, but as a servant appointed. The encounter is not punishment; it is commission. What Paul meant for evil, the Lord will use for good, and Paul will bear witness to what he has seen and what will be shown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Delivering you from the people, and from the Gentiles." He will be sent to both, and persecuted by both, yet the Lord Himself is Paul's shield and deliverer. The danger is real; so is the protection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Open eyes, turn from darkness to light, from Satan's power to God's, receive forgiveness and an inheritance. That is the whole gospel in one sentence: sight, turning, rescue, blessing. The same work the Lord did in Paul, He sends Paul to do for others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision." What obedience is this? Immediate, unquestioning, irrevocable. When the Lord appears, there is no bargaining—only the choice to follow or turn away. Paul chose the cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Damascus to Jerusalem to Judea to the Gentiles—Paul fills the geography with the gospel. Works worthy of repentance: not many works, but true ones, rooted in a turned heart. The Lord measures fruit by depth, not display.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jews seized him in the temple and tried to kill him. The same people he defended, the same city he loved—now they hunt him. Love and opposition can live in the same place; grace and fury can occupy the same moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Having obtained help from God, I stand to this day." Paul speaks directly to Agrippa's court as he would to any king: not as a prisoner begging mercy, but as a man upheld by the Almighty, testifying to both small and great without fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Christ must suffer; by resurrection He will proclaim light to Jews and Gentiles alike. Paul strings the whole promise together: suffering, rising, witness—the very shape of his own life. He has become what he preaches.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Festus interrupts, loud and mocking: "Your learning is driving you mad!" The world has always mistaken the gospel for madness. Festus thinks Paul crazy; Paul knows the resurrection real. They are measuring by different scales.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul is calm, respectful, "most excellent Festus." He does not match Festus's mockery with defensiveness; he speaks truth and reason quietly. The meek inherit the earth—sometimes they inherit a hearing, too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "The king knows of these things... this has not been done in a corner." Paul appeals to shared knowledge: the resurrection, the witnesses, the reports—all public, not hidden. He invites Agrippa to see what he already knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Do you believe the prophets?" A master stroke—Paul turns to what Agrippa knows and holds dear, and asks: do you believe your own scriptures? The king cannot say no without denying his faith; he cannot say yes without admitting the gospel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Agrippa's reply is almost playful: "With little persuasion you are trying to make me a Christian." He feels the weight of the truth; he knows he stands at a threshold. Yet knowing and stepping through are two different things.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's prayer: whether with little or much, not only Agrippa but all who hear him today, become such as I am—except for these bonds. He wishes his chains on no one, yet wishes his faith on everyone. That is the heart of an apostle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king rose up with the governor and Bernice. The hearing is over. Paul has spoken; Agrippa has heard. The door closes—not in fury, but in silence. Sometimes the Lord's word falls into soil that will not yield, not yet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They admit: "This man does nothing worthy of death or bonds." Paul's words have won a verdict from the powerful themselves. Yet he remains imprisoned. Justice and the will of man do not always align; Paul trusts a higher court.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Agrippa tells Festus: Paul could have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar. Readers today hear an echo in that: Paul's own choice, his faithfulness to his calling even through captivity, shapes the arc of his witness. Some chains are locks to the world; some open doors to the kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
